64.title: He washes their feet (John 13:1–17)
64.hook: the teacher kneels with a towel and washes twelve pairs of dusty feet
64.howItsDone: On Maundy Thursday, the Thursday before Easter, many Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Protestant churches wash feet during the service. Some traditions, including many Brethren and Mennonite churches, practice foot washing regularly with communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, spikenard: a whole pound poured on his feet, and love can be lavish. Today, feet again, and this time he's the one kneeling.

The bathroom nobody cleans. The leaking trash bag. The diaper at three in the morning. Every house has jobs that wait for someone else. Tonight, a room in Jerusalem, before the feast of the Passover. Roads were dust and dirt, and sandals don't keep much out. In the Bible, washing feet is servant's work; in the book of Samuel, Abigail offers to do it as a handmaid. John mentions no servant here. He says that during supper, their teacher stands up from the table.
screen: `THE JOBS NOBODY WANTS.` → `DUSTY ROADS, OPEN SANDALS.` → `THE TEACHER STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: John opens with a line about love, in the King James Bible: "having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end." Then Jesus gets up from supper, lays aside his outer clothes, and ties a towel around his waist, dressed like a servant. "After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded." One pair of feet after another, including the feet of Judas, who's about to betray him. Then he comes to Peter, and Peter can't bear it: "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus answers: "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me." And Peter, all or nothing as always, swings the other way: "Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head." Afterward Jesus dresses, sits down, and asks: do you know what I've done to you? You call me master and lord, and you're right. "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet." I've given you an example. Later that night he gives them a new commandment: love one another, as I have loved you. In Latin, commandment is mandatum, and the name Maundy Thursday, the Thursday before Easter, is said to come from it. On that day some churches still wash feet, and popes have knelt with a basin too. Among the Brethren, some Mennonites and others, foot washing is part of the communion service. The one who ends up with a crown of thorns starts the night with a towel.

65.title: The last supper (Luke 22:14–20)
65.hook: bread broken, a cup shared, and "do this in remembrance of me"
65.howItsDone: Nearly all Christians share bread and wine, or grape juice, in memory of the Last Supper, called the Eucharist, Holy Communion, the Lord's Supper, the Mass or the Divine Liturgy. Some churches celebrate it every day or every Sunday, others monthly or a few times a year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a teacher with a towel, kneeling at his friends' feet. Today, the same night, the meal itself.

A meal you'll never forget. Maybe the last dinner with someone before they moved away, or before they died. You didn't know it was the last one, or maybe you did. You remember where everyone sat. Now, an upstairs room in Jerusalem at Passover, the feast when Jewish families remember how God brought their ancestors out of slavery in Egypt, with bread and wine and the old story told again. Jesus sits down with his friends. And he knows this is the last time.
screen: `A MEAL YOU'LL NEVER FORGET.` → `AN UPSTAIRS ROOM AT PASSOVER.` → `HE KNOWS IT'S THE LAST TIME.`

segments.voice: Luke gives his first words at the table, in the King James Bible: "With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you before I suffer." That doubling is a Hebrew way of saying, I have longed and longed for this. Then he does what the head of the table did at a Jewish meal: takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and hands it around. But then he says something no one had heard at Passover before: "This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me." And after supper, the cup: "This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you." Testament here means covenant, a binding promise between God and people, like the one made with Israel at Sinai. The big word is remembrance; in Greek, anamnesis. It means more than recalling a fact. At Passover, Jewish families speak as if they themselves came out of Egypt; the past becomes present at the table. Christians have shared this meal ever since, and understand it differently. Catholics and Orthodox Christians believe the bread and wine truly become Christ's body and blood. Lutherans speak of Christ truly present in, with and under the bread and wine. Many Reformed Christians speak of a real spiritual presence. Many Baptists and others see it as a memorial, a powerful act of remembering. The names differ too: the Eucharist, from the Greek for gave thanks; Holy Communion; the Lord's Supper; the Mass; the Divine Liturgy. What almost all of them share is the table, the bread, the cup, and his words: do this, and remember me.

66.title: Gethsemane (Luke 22:39–46)
66.hook: in a garden at night he prays, sweating, not my will but yours
66.howItsDone: Many churches keep a watch on the night of Maundy Thursday, staying up to pray in memory of Gethsemane, and some Christians keep a holy hour of prayer on other nights. Pilgrims to Jerusalem visit an olive garden on the Mount of Olives with very old trees.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last supper: bread, a cup, anamnesis, and remember me. After the meal, they sing, and walk out into the dark.

The night before surgery. The night before a hard goodbye. Lying awake, bargaining with the ceiling. Across the brook Cedron from Jerusalem rises the Mount of Olives, and late this night Jesus goes there, Luke says, as he often did, and his disciples follow. Matthew and Mark name the place: Gethsemane. John calls it a garden. Tradition says the name means oil press, where olives are crushed. Tonight he's the one being pressed.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE THE DREADED THING.` → `THE MOUNT OF OLIVES, LATE.` → `GETHSEMANE: THE OIL PRESS.`

segments.voice: He tells his friends to pray that they don't fall into testing. Then he goes a stone's throw away, kneels, and prays, in the King James Bible: "Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." Notice what he asks first: take it away. He doesn't pretend he wants to suffer; he asks, honestly, for another way. In Isaiah and Jeremiah, a cup can stand for suffering and judgment. Only then: nevertheless, the word Simon said over his empty nets. Not my will, but yours. In Mark he calls God Abba, the family word for father. Then Luke gives a detail: "And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground." As it were: Luke may mean his sweat fell heavy as blood, or that it was mixed with blood; readers have taken it both ways. And a small honesty: some readers point out that these verses, with the angel who comes to strengthen him, are not in every early copy of Luke. Agony is Luke's Greek word, agonia, also used for the strain of a contest, a wrestler's or a runner's. And his friends? He comes back and finds them asleep, Luke says, sleeping for sorrow, and wakes them with a question: "Why sleep ye? rise and pray, lest ye enter into temptation." The shape of the prayer is plain: say what you want, all of it, and then, nevertheless.

segments.voice: Bring to mind the hardest thing in front of you, something you'd take away if you could, and silently say what you really want, all of it, without dressing it up: take it away, make it different, let me off. Then, if you can, notice what it would be like to hold it a little more loosely; you don't have to get to nevertheless today. If you pray, you can pray it to God just as honestly.

67.title: The rooster crows (Luke 22:54–62)
67.hook: Peter swears three times he never knew him, then the rooster, then the look
67.howItsDone: Peter's denial is read in Holy Week in many churches, and it's sung in the Passion settings of Bach and others. Weathervanes shaped like roosters sit on some church steeples, especially in Europe.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gethsemane: take this cup, and then, not my will. That same night, soldiers come to the garden.

Pretending not to know someone. Laughing along. Keeping quiet when you meant to speak. It can happen in a second, before anyone has decided anything. A courtyard in Jerusalem, in the middle of the night. Jesus has been arrested and taken into the high priest's house. Mark says the others fled. But Peter, who walked on water, who said he'd go to prison and to death with him, follows at a distance. He slips into the courtyard and sits down by a fire with the servants and guards, warming his hands.
screen: `PRETENDING NOT TO KNOW SOMEONE.` → `ARRESTED IN THE NIGHT.` → `PETER BY THE FIRE.`

segments.voice: A servant girl looks at him in the firelight and says: this man was with him. And Peter, in the King James Bible: "Woman, I know him not." A little later someone else: you're one of them. "Man, I am not." About an hour later, a third person insists: surely this fellow was with him, for he's a Galilean. And Peter says: "Man, I know not what thou sayest." While he's still speaking, the rooster crows. Earlier that evening Jesus had told him exactly this, and Peter had said never. Then Luke adds a detail no other Gospel has: "And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter." Across the courtyard, their eyes meet. Luke doesn't describe the look. Angry? Sad? Loving? The sources are silent. "And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And Peter went out, and wept bitterly." This story is in all four Gospels. The first Christians could have left out the night Peter failed; all four kept it. Peter, the rock, the one with the keys, is also the one who said three times, I don't know him. And failure isn't where his story ends. Tradition links the rooster on top of some church steeples to this night: a reminder to stay awake, and that even Peter fell, and was not finished.

Think of Peter weeping in the dark, whose story didn't end there, and say to yourself quietly: that happened, and I'm more than that. If you pray, you can ask to be forgiven and to forgive yourself.

68.title: Pilate and Simon (Luke 23:13–26)
68.hook: a governor washes his hands; a passer-by from Cyrene is made to carry the cross
68.tomorrow: At the foot of the cross
68.howItsDone: Many Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches pray the Stations of the Cross in Lent, walking or meditating on fourteen moments of Jesus's last journey; Simon of Cyrene helping to carry the cross is the fifth. Christians often recite in the creeds that he suffered under Pontius Pilate.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cock crow, and Peter weeping by the fire. Now, two very different men step in.

Some hard days have two kinds of people: the one with power to stop what's happening, and the one who happens to be walking by. One decides; the other can only help carry it. Jerusalem, in the morning. After a night of questioning, Jesus is brought to the Roman governor, Pontius Pilate. Crucifixion is a Roman punishment, and the order will be his. Outside the city, a man from North Africa is walking in from the countryside, with no idea what's coming.
screen: `THE ONE WITH POWER, THE ONE PASSING BY.` → `PONTIUS PILATE, IN THE MORNING.` → `ROME'S PUNISHMENT, PILATE'S ORDER.`

segments.voice: Pilate questions Jesus and says to the chief priests and the crowd, in the King James Bible: "I find no fault in this man." In Luke he says it three times. He sends Jesus to Herod Antipas, who mocks him and sends him back. Pilate offers to have him whipped and let go. But the crowd shouts for Barabbas, in prison for rebellion and murder: "Crucify him, crucify him." And Pilate, who has the power, gives in. He releases Barabbas and hands Jesus over to be crucified. The famous hand-washing is in Matthew, not Luke: Pilate washes his hands before the crowd and says: "I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it." But water doesn't wash away a decision. The order was Pilate's, and Roman soldiers carried it out. For centuries some Christians wrongly blamed the Jewish people as a whole; the Catholic Church rejected that blame plainly at the Second Vatican Council, and other churches have too. Then Luke turns to Simon: "And as they led him away, they laid hold upon one Simon, a Cyrenian, coming out of the country, and on him they laid the cross, that he might bear it after Jesus." Cyrene was in North Africa, in what is now Libya, and Acts mentions Jews from there in Jerusalem. Some readers think Simon was a pilgrim in town for the feast. He didn't volunteer: Luke says they laid hold on him. But Mark names his sons, Alexander and Rufus, and some readers think the first audience knew them. If so, the man forced to carry the cross became part of the story.

If you pray, you can hold them before God.

69.title: At the foot of the cross (John 19:25–30)
69.hook: his mother stands there, and he gives her and John to each other
69.howItsDone: On Good Friday, many churches read the Passion from John's Gospel, and some hold three hours of prayer and silence in the afternoon. The Stabat Mater is sung in many churches, and Catholics and others remember Our Lady of Sorrows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pilate and Simon: the man with the power, and the Cyrenian who carried the cross. Today, the hardest place in the story.

At a hospital bed there can come a point where there's nothing left to do. No more phone calls, no more questions for the doctor. Just being there. Staying. Outside Jerusalem is a place John calls Golgotha, the place of a skull, and a Roman cross. Over it hangs the title Pilate wrote: Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews. Standing near a man Rome was executing under that title can't have been safe. But John says a small group stands near the cross anyway.
screen: `BY A HOSPITAL BED.` → `GOLGOTHA, OUTSIDE THE CITY.` → `A FEW WHO STAYED.`

segments.voice: John names them, in the King James Bible: "Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene." Mostly women, and one man John never names, only calls the disciple whom Jesus loved; Christian tradition has long said this was John himself. And there is Mary, his mother: the one who said let it be to the angel, who wrapped him in cloths and laid him in a manger, who heard Simeon say a sword would pierce her own soul. Now she's here. Jesus, in terrible pain, looks down and takes care of her. "Woman, behold thy son!" And to the disciple: "Behold thy mother!" And John says: "And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home." Even on the cross he's making sure his mother won't be alone. Some read more here too: Catholics and Orthodox Christians often see Mary given as a mother to every disciple. Then he says: "I thirst." They lift a sponge of sour wine to his mouth. And then three words in English, one in Greek: "It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost." The Greek is tetelestai: finished, completed, accomplished, brought to its end. Not I'm finished, as in defeated. It is finished, as in done, the work completed. Christians have long sung a Latin hymn about this scene called Stabat Mater, the mother was standing. Because that's what she did. She couldn't stop it or fix it. She stood there. She stayed.

70.howItsDone: Christians celebrate the resurrection at Easter, the most important feast of the Christian year, often with a vigil or a sunrise service. The Catholic Church keeps Mary Magdalene's feast on July 22, calling her the apostle to the apostles, and Orthodox Christians honor her as equal to the apostles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tetelestai, and the few who stayed by the cross. He was buried in a garden tomb before the Sabbath. Now it's the first day of the week, still dark.

Grief makes you do strange things. You drive past their house. You keep their voicemail. You go back to the last place they were. Mary Magdalene goes to the tomb while it's still dark. She had traveled with Jesus and supported him; Luke says he had freed her from seven demons. She stood at the cross. And now she finds the stone rolled away and the tomb empty. She runs for Peter and the beloved disciple; they come, look, and go home. But Mary stays outside the tomb, weeping.

segments.voice: She stoops to look in: two angels in white, sitting where his body had been. They ask why she weeps; she says, in the King James Bible: "Because they have taken away my Lord, and I know not where they have laid him." She turns, and someone is standing there. "Woman, why weepest thou? whom seekest thou?" She thinks he's the gardener: "Sir, if thou have borne him hence, tell me where thou hast laid him, and I will take him away." She doesn't recognize him. Her eyes are full of tears, and the dead don't stand in gardens. Then one word: "Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master." That's the moment: not a sermon, not a proof, just her name. Rabboni means my teacher, a word of closeness. He tells her not to cling to him and sends her to the others; she goes and says: "I have seen the Lord." This is the heart of Christian faith: that Jesus rose from the dead. And in John the first person to see him, and the first sent to tell it, is a woman who stayed when the others went home. Early Christian writers called her the apostle to the apostles. One myth to clear away: the Bible never says she was a prostitute. That idea came from a sermon centuries later that mixed her up with other women in the Gospels.
